register: Step 12 target register — every named deferral in the spec's §2 table, with a TYPED disposition
rule: A target may not close untyped. The disposition vocabulary is closed, and each type carries the evidence its own claim requires: fixed-and-pinned needs a test, pinned-as-fact needs a written reason, owned-and-deferred needs a named owner step, inconclusive-fail-closed needs the fail-closed action actually taken. The meta-test (scripts/step12-targets.test.ts) enforces both the vocabulary and the evidence, and pins the row set so the table cannot quietly shrink.

dispositions.fixed-and-pinned: reproduced as a defect, fixed, and pinned by a test that fails without the fix
dispositions.pinned-as-fact: attempted and NOT reproducible as a defect; the property that defeated it is pinned by a test, or the limitation is a stated fact of the design
dispositions.owned-and-deferred: real, not closed here; carried by a named owner step with a verifiable exit
dispositions.inconclusive-fail-closed: could not be determined; the fail-closed action was taken rather than the hopeful one

rows.title: Injection-string corpus over tool RESULTS — rules-bypass, role-confusion, nested SYSTEM: framing
rows.reason: Attempted across three independent corpora and not reproducible as a control failure: golden fixture 04 records the injected text verbatim as DATA and the pore still fires; the 29 catalog packages each carry three hostile payloads proven against a real suspending run; and the T9 probe delivers an injected instruction through the ordinary result path. The structural floor holds because the gate does not consult the result. What a corpus cannot settle is whether a real model COMPLIES — that is T9, and it rides the live leg.

rows.title: Malicious MCP server protocol fuzzing — malformed JSON-RPC, oversized/slow streams, capability lying
rows.reason: Attempted with five malformed result shapes plus surface-lying and mid-session surface change. Every case returns a TYPED value and never throws into the loop, which is the contract mcp-tools.ts states in its header. A server that advertises tools we never authored cannot widen its surface, because discovery is an intersection with the authored allowlist; a server that changes its surface mid-session reaches nothing, because the leg's tools are bound once at leg start.

rows.title: Exfiltration THROUGH tool arguments — the model induced to send data outward
rows.reason: REPRODUCED, and it was the pass's critical finding (L2). The pore showed the operator `publish({body:'first'})`; on resume the model emitted `publish({body:'second — never approved'})` and it executed ungated — the approval authorized 'the next external action', not the action displayed. The fix went further than the fingerprint it started with: the resumed leg now REPLAYS the approved call from the check-in record instead of asking the model to re-propose it, because with a real model the re-proposal never matches and the pore would re-ask forever.

rows.title: Cross-connector interaction attacks — one grant's data reaching another's call
rows.reason: Attempted and not reproducible. Sessions are per-connector and each carries only its own bearer — asserted over the servers' recorded authorization headers, both directions. And the redactor is built over the WHOLE leg's held secrets, so connector A echoing connector B's token is scrubbed before the checkpoint, which the second test proves by handing A a token it could not otherwise know.

rows.title: Split-token echo ACROSS multiple results — every shard below the fragment floor
rows.reason: REPRODUCED against the stateless redactor: four results of eleven characters each hand over the whole credential and not one shard is recognized. Closed by the leg-stateful reassembly sentinel, which observes what survived the scrub, accumulates the secret offsets that escaped, and trips at SPLIT_TOKEN_MIN_MATCH — no leg may lose more of a secret across results than one scrubbed fragment would have revealed inside one. On the trip the result is withheld and the connector is cut for the leg.

rows.title: Sub-shard reassembly — shards under SPLIT_TOKEN_MIN_MATCH, including interleaved and out-of-order
rows.reason: REPRODUCED inside a single result with scrambled pieces, and closed by the same sentinel, which counts shards wherever they appear — one result or many, in object keys as well as values, in any order, because ordering is the attacker's choice and not evidence of innocence. The residual is MEASURED rather than denied: shards shorter than SHARD_MIN_MATCH are under the detector, which costs an attacker one metered tool call per four characters of credential, and up to eleven offsets escape before the trip.
rows.evidence: packages/lab-mcp/src/reassembly.test.ts (including the 'shards BELOW the floor evade' case that records the limit); golden fixture 09

rows.title: Arbitrary/layered transforms of a held token — gzip+base64, rot-N, custom encodings
rows.reason: Not fixable by a known-value scrub, and Step 12 says so rather than implying coverage it does not have. The redactor owns the standard whole-token encodings a real echo reaches for (raw, base64, base64url, unpadded, URL, hex) and the sentinel owns shard reassembly of the RAW value; an arbitrary transform defeats both by construction, because the transformed bytes share nothing with the secret. The compensating controls are named and real — the Step 3 pattern gate on credential SHAPES, and the pore on every outward action — but they are compensations, not coverage.
rows.owner: external review before customer credentials at scale (spec §10 non-coverage)

rows.title: The act/read classification audit — all 116 classifications against real vendor semantics
rows.reason: Audited every tool with four independent reviewers over disjoint slices; each row names the vendor operation and rates its own confidence. Five read tools could not be shown inert and lean act — sentry.get_issue (writes a GroupSeen row), salesforce.soql_query (FOR VIEW / FOR REFERENCE write LastViewedDate), dropbox.get_file (may mint a public temporary link), discord.read_messages (acks the channel; messages.read is not a REST scope), zoom.get_transcript (mints a download credential) — and every one was reclassified to act rather than left a read we merely hope about. The audit's own bound is published with it: no verdict checked a NAME against a live server, because every package is fixture-authored.
rows.failClosedAction: 5 tools reclassified read → act; 7 packages version-bumped; dropbox and discord lost a default scope; salesforce's fictional api_write and google-drive's unusable drive.file corrected; pagerduty's inverted description fixed; funded acts now require a written vendor-limit reason (scopeLimits) in both the validator and the least-privilege test

rows.title: Live-model persuasion resistance — does a REAL model obey an injected instruction?
rows.reason: Cannot be evidenced against a mock model at all, so the probe rides the live leg's budget as the operator directed. The probe is built, rehearsed, and reports both halves — whether the model ATTEMPTED the injected act, and whether the pore stopped it — but the behavioural half is unmeasured until the sitting happens. The structural half is already pinned at $0.
rows.owner: the operator sitting in this same step (spec §7); the probe runs inside the $1 leg
rows.evidence: scripts/step10-live-mcp.ts (T9 persuasion probe); rehearsal output shows the mock-model half

rows.title: Master key in the worker environment — the custody perimeter spans two processes
rows.reason: True and unchanged: the worker needs the master key to open a grant, so the key is in a second process's environment. Nothing in this pass narrows that; a managed key service is a deployment capability, not a code change.
rows.owner: Step 13 — deploy (KMS/secret manager for POTION_MASTER_KEY; the env-var path is the local/dev posture)

rows.title: Provider-side rate limits and billing are the vendor's; our caps bound our side only
rows.reason: A statement of scope, not a defect: our per-tool call/byte/dollar caps bound what WE do with a grant. They cannot bound what the vendor charges or throttles, and no code we write can. Recorded so nobody later reads 'caps' as covering the vendor's meter.

rows.title: Attributed spend is PROVISIONAL — the est cost of the model steps that emitted the calls
rows.reason: Re-examined and still provisional: the attribution rule under-counts result-processing tokens and over-counts multi-intent steps. It is LABELLED provisional in the code and the label is pin-tested so it cannot be quietly detached. Re-deriving it needs observed live per-tool traffic, which this step does not produce.
rows.evidence: packages/lab-mcp/src/caps.ts attributedEstUsd (the pinned ATTRIBUTION RULE note)

rows.title: Fuel is denominated in the flat token-rate ESTIMATE — premium rungs can meter above maxUsdPerRun
rows.reason: Real and unresolved here: the run-level hard stop trips on an estimate, so a premium model's true cost can exceed the declared ceiling before the estimate catches up. The honest fix is reconciliation against request_logs (the metered join already exists for reporting) driving the stop, which is metering work rather than adversarial work.
rows.owner: Step 13 — deploy (metered-spend reconciliation drives the hard stop, not the estimate)

rows.title: lab:run reads the catalog row per invocation for clusterHint — an in-place edit can redirect remaining legs
rows.reason: Confirmed structurally: the hint is re-read each invocation, so an admin edit between legs changes routing mid-run. It is an org-admin capability affecting only that org's own run, and the spec identity (content hash) does not move — which is exactly why it deserves an owner rather than silence.
rows.owner: Step 13 — deploy (pin the routing inputs into the run record at start, alongside the spec snapshot)

rows.title: A worker crash mid-leg leaves the run 'running' until the lease expires
rows.reason: This is the lease doing its job, not a defect: the claim is fenced and time-bounded, so a crashed invocation's work cannot be resumed by anyone until its lease lapses, and the fence rejects a late writer outright. The visible cost is a window where the run reads 'running' with nobody working it. The alternative — trusting a crashed process to tidy up — is worse.
rows.evidence: packages/db/src/repos/lab-runs.ts (claimLabRun / LabFenceError); the fence rejection is exercised in the live script's cap proof

rows.title: lab:run executes user-authored missions in worker processes
rows.reason: By design and bounded: a mission is prose the model reads, not code the worker runs. What it can reach is bounded by fuel, per-leg caps, the per-tool caps, the serving gates, and the pore on every outward action. There is no eval path and no user-supplied code path; the risk is spend and outward action, both metered and gated.

rows.title: Filed guarantee-product debt a Lab path can reach: F8, F9, F13, F14, F15, F16, F17, F18
rows.reason: Re-examined for Lab reachability rather than re-litigated. None is a Lab-surface defect and none blocks Gate C on the Lab's account; they remain filed against the guarantee product with their original severities, which is where they will be fixed.
